summary: Children aged 10-11 learn that about 97% of Earth's water is salt water, almost all of it in the oceans, and only about 3% (more precisely about 2.5%) is fresh, and that most of the fresh water is locked in glaciers/ice caps and groundwater, leaving only a tiny sliver as accessible surface water in rivers and lakes. The core move is to BUILD or READ a graph (bar or pie) of reservoir volumes so the striking proportions become visible evidence, then reason about why usable fresh water is precious. A nested 'zoom' representation (all water -> the 3% fresh -> the tiny liquid-surface fraction) is intended to make the scarcity concrete rather than merely stated.
misconceptions: 'There's plenty of fresh water' — not seeing that most fresh water is locked in ice/underground.
'Fresh water mostly means rivers and lakes' — overlooking glaciers and groundwater as the largest fresh stores.
'Salt and fresh water are roughly equal' — underestimating the 97% ocean share.
'Percentages on a graph are the actual volumes' — confusing proportion with amount when reading the chart.
'Ice caps aren't fresh water' — not classifying glacial ice as fresh.

activities.title: Build a reservoir graph, then zoom into the fresh-water slice
steps: Name each reservoir first (oceans, glaciers/ice caps, groundwater, rivers, lakes), then add its volume to a bar or pie chart one reservoir at a time; once all are added, notice that the ocean accounts for roughly 97% of the total (most of the pie, or a bar far taller than all the others combined).

Zoom into the thin ~3% 'fresh water' wedge so it fills the view, then divide that fresh slice again into its parts (mostly frozen ice caps/glaciers plus groundwater, with a hair-thin sliver of rivers and lakes).
Recompute or redraw the chart as reservoirs are included or excluded, so the proportions visibly change.

Separately, retell the same data as 100 water drops sorting themselves into about 97 salty and 3 fresh, and note how few of the fresh drops are actually reachable surface water (fewer than 1 of the 100).
State in your own words why accessible fresh water is limited, using the graph as your evidence.
activities.insight: The water people can actually reach (surface rivers and lakes) is a sliver of a sliver: only ~3% of all water is fresh, and most of that is frozen in ice caps/glaciers or held underground, which is why usable fresh water is precious.

activities.title: Hands-on beaker and 100-drops demonstration
steps: Fill a 1 litre container to represent all of Earth's water, then measure out about 30 ml to stand for the fresh water, leaving the remaining ~970 ml as the salty ocean share.
Set most of the fresh portion aside as 'frozen in ice caps' or 'underground', keeping only a few drops to represent the rivers and lakes we can easily use.
Describe what each quantity represents and compare the reachable sliver with the whole container.
Optionally re-tell the same split as 100 drops: about 97 salty, about 3 fresh, and fewer than 1 easily accessible.
activities.insight: A physical pour-off is intended to make the 97/3 proportion and the even smaller accessible fraction tangible, reinforcing the graph evidence.

activities.title: Read and reason from a supplied chart
steps: Given a pie or bar chart of reservoir volumes, estimate what percentage of Earth's water is fresh.
Order the reservoirs from largest to smallest by volume.
Match each reservoir (oceans, ice caps/glaciers, groundwater, rivers, lakes) to whether the chart counts it as salt or fresh water, noting that some lakes and some groundwater are actually salty.

From the chart, state where most fresh water is stored and explain the reasoning (teaching note: the largest single fresh store is frozen ice caps/glaciers, with groundwater the next-largest; very little is in surface rivers/lakes).
Respond to the prompt: 'A friend says most of the water on Earth is fresh water we can drink. Is that right?' Explain the actual amounts and where most of Earth's water sits.
activities.insight: Learners can interpret proportions and comparisons from a given graph and connect them to the real distribution of Earth's water, surfacing both the salt/fresh proportion error and the belief that visible surface water holds most fresh water.

activities.title: Motivating scaled-volume hook
steps: Look at a scaled visual such as all of Earth's water gathered into a single small sphere beside the globe, or stacked water tanks scaled to reservoir volumes.
Predict how big the fresh-water portion would be before revealing it.
Move on to building or reading the actual chart to quantify the proportions.
activities.insight: A dramatic scaled-volume image may spark curiosity about how little of Earth is water we can use, motivating the graphing work that quantifies it.

checkQuestion: Earth looks blue and covered in water from space. A friend says most of the water on Earth is fresh water we can drink. Is that right? Explain what the amounts actually are and where most of Earth's water is.
checkAnswer: The friend is wrong. About 97% of Earth's water is salty ocean water; only about 3% is fresh, and most of that is frozen in glaciers and ice caps or stored underground — so only a tiny fraction is in the rivers and lakes we can easily use.
